claims.text: Models show non-uniform performance degradation with context length—particularly on semantic matching tasks, where degradation rate depends on needle-question similarity, distractor density, and haystack structure. Semantic tasks degrade non-smoothly even when lexical-retrieval benchmarks pass, meaning real applications can fail at scale despite passing standard benchmarks.

claims.text: A single MCP server with 93 tools consumes approximately 55,000 tokens per turn in overhead before any user input. System prompts add 2,000–5,000 tokens per turn; each tool definition adds 500–1,400 tokens. Heavy configurations with five or more servers consume more than 50,000 tokens before the first prompt. Disabling unused servers and enabling them only when needed immediately reclaims this entire allocation.

claims.text: Automatic compaction at 95% context usage forces multiple compression cycles, each round discarding detail from earlier exchanges and degrading the model's ability to track early decisions. Manual compaction at 60% context usage produces better results by triggering fewer, more deliberate compressions. After two or three automatic compactions, the model becomes noticeably less accurate.

claims.text: Context degradation thresholds are defined by absolute token counts, not relative context fill—a 1M-token model at 40% capacity has consumed 400K tokens and is deeply degraded, while a 200K model at 40% has consumed only 80K tokens and remains fully functional. Measurable degradation begins around 100K-200K tokens for most models, independent of total window size, with significant quality loss accelerating beyond 200K tokens consumed.

claims.text: Distractor interference—semantically related but factually irrelevant content—is a primary driver of context rot distinct from and more damaging than missing information. Chroma's 2025 testing of 18 frontier models found that a single topically adjacent distractor reduces baseline performance, with the effect compounding non-uniformly as distractor count increases. In real coding tasks, this manifests acutely: grepping for a function returns multiple similar implementations from unrelated modules, each a plausible but wrong distractor that actively degrades subsequent reasoning more than if those results had simply not appeared.

claims.text: Across all 18 frontier models tested by Chroma in 2025, models performed measurably better on shuffled haystacks than on logically coherent documents. Well-organized, consistently-named code creates more semantically plausible distractors because adjacent files share terminology and concepts, making wrong answers more convincing to the attention mechanism. A well-organized codebase is paradoxically harder for an LLM to search accurately than a randomly arranged one.
